full_text_en:
Xu Minghong v. Quanzhou Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd. and Lin Shuzhe — dispute over company-related matters

Ruling Summary

I. A people's court shall, in accordance with the Company Law, the Judicial Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Company Law (IV), and the Civil Procedure Law, examine whether a party filing an action for confirmation of invalidity of a company resolution is a proper plaintiff. For a party who no longer holds the status of a shareholder or the position of director or supervisor at the time of filing the action, the people's court shall, pursuant to Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law, examine whether such party meets the conditions for filing an action, such as having a direct interest in the case.

II. A board resolution in the sense of the Company Law is a document reflecting the board of directors' commercial judgment and independent will, formed by the board of directors in accordance with the authority and voting procedures prescribed by law or the company's articles of association, following a vote on matters under deliberation. A documentary record made by the board of directors of a Sino-foreign equity joint venture regarding the appointment and removal of directors by a joint venture party in accordance with legal provisions does not constitute a board resolution in the sense of the Company Law, nor can it be the subject of an action for confirmation of invalidity of a company resolution.

Civil Ruling of the Supreme People's Court

(2017) Supreme People's Court Final No. 18

Appellant (plaintiff at first instance): Xu Minghong (formerly known as Xu Mingliang), male, born June 9, 1959, resident of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, residing in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Authorized litigation representatives: Yao Xiaomin, lawyer of Beijing Lantai Law Firm; Liu Xiaoxu, lawyer of Beijing Lantai Law Firm.

Respondent (defendant at first instance): Quanzhou Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd. Domicile: Water Park, Quanshan Road, Fengze District, Quanzhou City, Fujian Province.

Legal representative: Lin Shuzhe, chairman of the board of the company. Authorized litigation representatives: Wang Yunying, lawyer of Fujian Xinshitong Law Firm; Li Hao, lawyer of Beijing Tiantong (Nanjing) Law Firm.

Respondent (defendant at first instance): Lin Shuzhe, male, born September 18, 1948, resident of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, residing in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.

Authorized litigation representatives: Peng Qing, lawyer of Beijing Tiantong Law Firm; Lin Geng, lawyer of Grandall Law Firm (Fuzhou).

Appellant Xu Minghong filed an appeal with this Court against the civil ruling (2015) Min Min Chu Zi No. 123 of the Fujian High People's Court, in a dispute with respondents Quanzhou Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Quanzhou Nanming Company) and Lin Shuzhe over company-related matters. This Court formed a collegial panel in accordance with the law and held a public hearing. The authorized litigation representatives of appellant Xu Minghong, Yao Xiaomin and Liu Xiaoxu, the authorized litigation representatives of respondent Quanzhou Nanming Company, Wang Yunying and Li Hao, and the authorized litigation representatives of respondent Lin Shuzhe, Peng Qing and Lin Geng, appeared in court. The hearing of this case is now concluded.

Xu Minghong's grounds for appeal: To set aside the ruling of first instance and order the Fujian High People's Court to hear this case. Facts and reasons: (I) The ruling of first instance erred in finding facts. 1. The ruling of first instance erred in finding that the property formed after Xu Minghong and five other investors injected capital into Hong Kong Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Hong Kong Nanming Company) should belong to Hong Kong Nanming Company. The court of first instance did not investigate the facts concerning how Hong Kong Nanming Company handled the investment funds received from Xu Minghong and the other five investors. Without ascertaining whether the funds contributed by the six investors entered the assets of Hong Kong Nanming Company or whether the six investors merely used Hong Kong Nanming Company as an investment channel to invest in the name of that company, the court made the aforementioned finding prematurely. 2. The ruling of first instance erred in finding that even if Xu Minghong completed his capital contribution, he was only a de facto controller of Quanzhou Nanming Company, not a de facto investor. The de facto controller of a company is often consistent with the de facto investor; the two concepts are not contradictory. (II) The ruling of first instance erred in application of law. 1. The facts of Xu Minghong's actual capital contribution have been ascertained in this case, and Xu Minghong also submitted evidence to prove that his signature was forged, showing that he indeed has various interests in this case. The ruling of first instance dismissed Xu Minghong's action on the ground of improper subject status by applying Article 119 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Procedure Law), which does not comply with Article 22, Paragraph 1 of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Company Law). 2. The ruling of first instance, being a procedural ruling on dismissing the action, made findings on many substantive issues beyond the necessary factual scope for reaching the conclusion of the ruling, clearly exceeding the scope of its ruling authority and causing improper impact or even infringement on the substantive rights of the parties.

Quanzhou Nanming Company argued: Xu Minghong's grounds for appeal are untenable; the ruling of first instance had clear findings of fact and correct application of law and should be affirmed. (I) Xu Minghong explicitly stated that the basis for his claims was that "as a de facto investor, he made capital contributions to establish Quanzhou Nanming Company," but he failed to prove the capital contribution. Even if Xu Minghong did contribute to Hong Kong Nanming Company, based on the independent legal personality of the legal entity, the property formed after his contribution should belong to Hong Kong Nanming Company. Xu Minghong does not have shareholder status in Quanzhou Nanming Company, and his capital contribution cannot serve as the basis for exercising the rights claimed in this case. The handling of the investment funds by Hong Kong Nanming Company after receipt is irrelevant to this case. (II) The ruling of first instance found that Xu Minghong filed this lawsuit to assert shareholder rights, and Xu Minghong did not object to this. In this case, Xu Minghong has no evidence proving that he entrusted Hong Kong Nanming Company to make the investment. Even if Xu Minghong were a de facto investor, according to the Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Trial of Foreign-Invested Enterprise Disputes (I) (hereinafter referred to as the "Foreign Investment Judicial Interpretation (I)"), he does not have the right to bring this lawsuit. (III) Xu Minghong's claims require a specific identity as a prerequisite, and his alleged "various interests in this case" cannot cure his lack of standing. The exercise of his rights lacks legal basis. The content of the board resolution at issue pertains to internal corporate governance matters. Even if Xu Minghong believes he has an interest in it, this should be resolved separately with the shareholder who appointed him as a director. Similarly, regarding investment returns, this should also be resolved separately with Hong Kong Nanming Company, and he cannot directly assert rights against Quanzhou Nanming Company. (IV) Xu Minghong's claim that the ruling of first instance "exceeded the scope of its ruling authority" in substantive findings lacks factual basis and is not a proper ground for appeal. (V) Xu Minghong filed this lawsuit 15 years after the board resolution at issue was made, seeking a declaration of its invalidity. He knew that the law clearly provides for the exercise of rights by de facto investors, yet he insisted on bringing this lawsuit and made applications for evidence preservation, handwriting examination, and financial audit in the first instance, showing a tendency to abuse procedural rights.

Lin Shuzhe argued: The ruling of first instance had clear findings of fact and correct application of law; all of Xu Minghong's grounds for appeal are untenable. (I) Xu Minghong's claims for confirmation of the validity of the board resolution and for distribution of company earnings are respectively an action for confirmation and an action for payment. These two claims belong to different legal relationships and have no factual or legal connection. They do not constitute a joint action that can be consolidated for trial. Xu Minghong's assertion of both in one case lacks legal basis and should be dismissed. (II) Lin Shuzhe is merely the legal representative of Quanzhou Nanming Company, not a party with an interest in the board resolution at issue, nor does he enjoy any shareholder rights in Quanzhou Nanming Company. This dispute is unrelated to Lin Shuzhe. Xu Minghong's filing of the lawsuit against Lin Shuzhe is manifestly malicious, and the action against Lin Shuzhe should be dismissed. Other opinions are the same as those of Quanzhou Nanming Company in its defense.

Xu Minghong's claims at first instance: 1. To declare invalid the "Board Resolution of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd." dated August 9, 2000; 2. To order Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe to jointly and severally compensate Xu Minghong for economic losses, provisionally calculated at RMB 90 million (the final amount to be based on the audit or appraisal conducted by a relevant institution entrusted by the people's court); 3. To order Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe to jointly bear all litigation costs, preservation fees, and other expenses in this case.

Facts found by the court of first instance: I. On January 12, 1993, Hong Kong Nanming Company was incorporated and registered in Hong Kong. The shareholders were Xu Mingqi and Yang Lianjia, each holding one share. On November 28, 2006, Xu Mingqi transferred his one share to Xu Weifu.

II. On December 29, 1995, Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. was established. The registered capital of the company was RMB 20 million, and total investment was RMB 25 million. Among them, Quanzhou Licheng District Real Estate Development Company (hereinafter referred to as Licheng Company) contributed RMB 4.8 million, accounting for 24% of the shares; Quanzhou Beifeng Foreign Processing and Assembly Company (hereinafter referred to as Beifeng Company) contributed RMB 1.2 million, accounting for 6% of the shares; Hong Kong Nanming Company contributed RMB 14 million, accounting for 70% of the shares. Article 17 of Chapter Four of the company's articles of association provided that the joint venture shall establish a board of directors, which shall be the highest authority of the joint venture; Article 18 specified the functions and powers of the board of directors; Article 19 provided that the board of directors shall consist of eight directors, of which Party A (Licheng Company) shall appoint two, Party B (Beifeng Company) shall appoint two, and Party C (Hong Kong Nanming Company) shall appoint four; the term of office for directors shall be four years, and they may be reappointed. Article 21 provided that when Parties A, B, and C appoint or replace directors, they shall notify the board of directors in writing.

III. On October 4, 1996, Hong Kong Nanming Company held a board meeting and formed the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd." The minutes recorded that Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd., Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, Lin Wenlong, Huang Chaoyang, and Dai Xinmin formed Hong Kong Nanming Company through cooperation. Among them, Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd. held 50% of the shares, and Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, Lin Wenlong, Huang Chaoyang, and Dai Xinmin each held 10% of the shares. The company raised HKD 25 million, to be contributed in proportion to their respective shareholdings. The collection schedule was as follows: 1. On October 10, 1996, Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd. was to contribute HKD 5 million, and Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, and the other four were each to contribute HKD 1 million. 2. On December 31, 1996, Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd. was to contribute HKD 5 million, and Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, and the other four were each to contribute HKD 1 million. 3. On March 31, 1997, Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd. was to contribute HKD 2.5 million, and Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, and the other four were each to contribute HKD 500,000. Lin Shuzhe, Xu Weifu, Yang Lianjia, and Xu Mingliang all signed this board meeting minutes.

IV. On March 14, 1997, Quanzhou Quanlian Audit Office issued a "Report" on the verification of paid-in capital of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd., stating that Hong Kong Nanming Company remitted HKD 3,999,850 in October 1996, equivalent to RMB 4,285,839; it remitted HKD 4,999,700 in two installments in January 1997, equivalent to RMB 5,353,679; total RMB 9,639,518. On March 9, 1998, Quanzhou Quanlian Audit Office again issued a "Report" on the verification of paid-in capital of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd., stating that on May 5, 1997, the foreign investor remitted HKD 3,000,000, equivalent to RMB 3,214,200; total capital contributed in two installments amounted to RMB 12,853,718.

V. On December 2, 2003, Licheng Company and Beifeng Company respectively transferred all of their shares in Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. to Hong Kong Nanming Company. From then on, Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. became a wholly foreign-owned enterprise. On January 29, 2007, the name of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. was changed to Quanzhou Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd.

VI. In the case of Commercial Action No. 8 of 2013 in the Court of First Instance of the High Court of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, plaintiff Xu Mingqi v. defendants Lin Shuzhe, Nanyi Industry (Group) Co., Ltd., Hong Kong Nanming Company, Yang Lianjia, Xu Weifu, Haoyun Business Management Co., Ltd., and Shanghai Zhantian International Logistics Co., Ltd., the defense submitted by Hong Kong Nanming Company mentioned: "6. ... On or about January 12, 1993, Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd. was established in Hong Kong as an investment vehicle for the water park. Mr. Yang (Yang Lianjia) held one share of Nanming on behalf of the Group. As for the plaintiff (Xu Mingqi), with the consent of the younger brother of the Xu family, it was proposed that the plaintiff hold the other share of Nanming [but Mr. Lin (Lin Shuzhe) was not aware of the internal distribution of interests or family property arrangements between the plaintiff and the Xu brothers, nor did the Xu brothers disclose any relevant information to Mr. Lin or ask Mr. Lin to participate in related matters (if any)]... 18. The plaintiff (Xu Mingqi) paid (or arranged to pay) the first installment of HKD 1 million (due on October 10, 1996) on November 5, 1996. The plaintiff paid (or arranged to pay) the second installment of HKD 1 million (due on December 31, 1996) on March 6, 1997. However, the plaintiff subsequently failed to pay (or arrange to pay) the final installment of HKD 500,000 by the stipulated due date of March 31, 1997, or any other due date."

VII. Xu Minghong, formerly known as Xu Mingliang, changed his name to Xu Minghong on March 11, 2003.

The court of first instance held: In this case, Xu Minghong's first claim was for a declaration that the board resolution was invalid; his second claim, although expressed as a request for Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe to compensate for economic losses, was in substance a request for distribution of company earnings in proportion to his claimed capital contribution as a de facto investor. Both claims pertained to the assertion of shareholder rights, and the cause of action should be determined as a dispute over company-related matters. Since both Xu Minghong and Lin Shuzhe are residents of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, this case involves a civil and commercial dispute with Hong Kong elements and should be subject to centralized jurisdiction rules applicable to foreign-related cases. As all parties invoked the law of Mainland China during the proceedings and raised no objection to the application of law, the law of Mainland China should be confirmed as the governing law for this case.

Regarding Xu Minghong's standing to sue, Xu Minghong claimed that as a de facto investor, he made capital contributions to establish Quanzhou Nanming Company. Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe argued that both of Xu Minghong's claims were rights that only a shareholder could exercise, and Xu Minghong was not a shareholder of Quanzhou Nanming Company, therefore he was not a proper plaintiff in this case. The court of first instance held: (I) Based on the "Remittance Slip of Industrial Bank Co., Ltd. Hong Kong Branch" submitted by Xu Minghong, there was no indication that the HKD 2 million was paid by Xu Minghong. Moreover, Xu Minghong claimed that an additional HKD 500,000 was paid in cash, but he failed to provide any evidence. Although the defense submitted by Hong Kong Nanming Company in the Hong Kong litigation acknowledged receipt of HKD 2 million, it claimed that the payment was made by Xu Mingqi. Analyzing the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd.," it merely reflected the agreement among Hong Kong Nanfang Textile Co., Ltd., Xu Mingliang, Liu Sanhuang, Lin Wenlong, Huang Chaoyang, and Dai Xinmin to jointly contribute HKD 25 million to form Hong Kong Nanming Company. These board minutes only demonstrated the agreed capital contributions by the six investors to Hong Kong Nanming Company and did not reflect the actual investment situation of the six investors. Xu Minghong's claim that he contributed HKD 2.5 million lacked sufficient evidence. (II) Xu Minghong argued that the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd." was an agreement among the six investors regarding the investment in Quanzhou Nanming Company, and that the actual time and total amount of the Hong Kong party's registered capital contribution to Quanzhou Nanming Company were highly consistent with the agreement in the board minutes, making Xu Minghong a de facto investor in Quanzhou Nanming Company. However, according to Article 3 of the Company Law, a company has independent legal personality. As a lawfully established company, Hong Kong Nanming Company is independent in terms of property and liability from its promoters, directors, and members, and has an independent legal status. It should enjoy civil rights and assume civil obligations in its own name. Even if Xu Minghong paid HKD 2.5 million, the property formed after his contribution should belong to Hong Kong Nanming Company. Hong Kong Nanming Company, Beifeng Company, and Licheng Company are the registered shareholders and capital contributors of Quanzhou Nanming Company. (III) The six investors reflected in the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Real Estate Co., Ltd." were not themselves registered shareholders of Hong Kong Nanming Company. They only invested in Hong Kong Nanming Company by agreement, and then Hong Kong Nanming Company invested in the establishment of Quanzhou Nanming Company, thereby indirectly controlling the interests of Quanzhou Nanming Company. Even if the six investors actually completed their capital contributions as agreed, they collectively acted as de facto controllers of Quanzhou Nanming Company, rather than as silent investors in Quanzhou Nanming Company. This should not be characterized as entrusted investment and does not fall within the situation of "an agreement between parties whereby one party actually invests and the other party acts as a nominal shareholder of a foreign-invested enterprise" as provided in Article 14 of the Foreign Investment Judicial Interpretation (I).

In conclusion, the court of first instance held that Xu Minghong's claim that he was a de facto investor in Quanzhou Nanming Company was insufficiently supported by evidence. Since he was not a shareholder of Quanzhou Nanming Company, he could not exercise the property and other rights that only a shareholder of Quanzhou Nanming Company could enjoy, and therefore he was not a proper plaintiff in this case. As the court had not conducted a substantive review of Xu Minghong's claims, the matters involved in Xu Minghong's application for witnesses to testify in court also did not affect the determination of standing in this case. Therefore, his applications for investigation and evidence collection, handwriting examination, entrusted audit, and witness testimony were also not granted. In accordance with Article 119 and Article 154, Paragraph 1, Item 3 of the Civil Procedure Law, and Article 208, Paragraph 3 of the Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on the Application of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter referred to as the Civil Procedure Law Judicial Interpretation), the court ruled to dismiss Xu Minghong's action, and the case acceptance fee of RMB 491,800 pre-collected at first instance was refunded.

This Court finds through trial the following facts:

1. On August 9, 2000, Hong Kong Nanming Company issued a "Letter of Appointment" stating: "The original Chairman of Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd., Mr. Lin Shuzhe, and Hong Kong directors, Mr. Xu Mingliang and Mr. Guo Wenqiang, are no longer serving as directors of Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. due to work transfers and health reasons. Mr. Wang Mingde is hereby appointed as Chairman of Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd.; Mr. Liu Sanhuang and Mr. Wan Bisong are appointed as Hong Kong directors of Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd. The original director, Mr. Wu Changmou, remains unchanged."

2. The "Resolution of the Board of Directors of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd." dated August 9, 2000, states: "Members of the Board of Directors of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd., Lin Shuzhe, Guo Wenqiang, Xu Mingliang (originally written as Xu Mingyang), Yang Wuxi, Wan Xiangxin, Wu Qunde, and Zhang Zhaoxian, are no longer serving as directors of the company due to work transfers or health reasons. Upon study and decision by the Board of Directors, the director personnel are replaced as follows: Wang Mingde (Hong Kong director, serving as Chairman), Liu Sanhuang (Hong Kong director, serving as General Manager), Wan Bisong (Hong Kong director), Yan Chengcan (Chinese director), Yang Shaochuan (Chinese director), Zheng Yuexin (Chinese director), Guo Xiaoyang (Chinese director). The original Hong Kong director and General Manager, Mr. Wu Changmou, is no longer General Manager but remains a director. Resolved as such." The signatures at the conclusion of the board members include Lin Shuzhe, Yang Wuxi, Wan Xiangxin, Wu Changmou, and Xu Mingliang. Xu Minghong claims that the signature of "Xu Mingliang" here is forged.

3. Article 18 of Chapter 4 of the Articles of Association of Quanzhou Nanming Company provides: "The Board of Directors decides all major matters of the joint venture. Its main authorities are as follows: (1) Decide and approve important reports submitted by the General Manager (such as production plans, annual business reports, funds, loans, etc.); (2) Approve annual financial statements, revenue and expenditure budgets, and annual profit distribution plans; (3) Adopt important company rules and regulations; (4) Decide on the establishment of branches; (5) Amend company rules; (6) Discuss and decide on the suspension, termination, or merger of the joint venture with another economic organization; (7) Decide on the appointment of senior officers such as the General Manager and Accountant; (8) Be responsible for the liquidation of the joint venture upon its termination or expiration; (9) Other major matters that should be decided by the Board of Directors." Except for the facts stated above, the facts found in the First Instance ruling are true and are confirmed by this Court.

This Court holds that:

1. Regarding the applicable law for the dispute in this case. Xu Minghong and Lin Shuzhe are residents of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of the People's Republic of China. They filed and defended the lawsuit within Mainland China, and both invoked the laws of Mainland China for their claims and defenses during the proceedings. Therefore, the First Instance Court's determination that this case is a civil and commercial dispute involving Hong Kong, which should be tried with reference to the procedures for foreign-related cases, and that the applicable law for this case is the laws of Mainland China, complies with Article 19 and Article 8, Paragraph 2 of the "Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Law of the People's Republic of China on the Application of Laws to Foreign-related Civil Relations (I)". This Court upholds this determination.

2. Regarding whether the two claims in this case can be heard together. In this case, Xu Minghong filed a lawsuit with the First Instance Court on the grounds that the "Resolution of the Board of Directors of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd." dated August 9, 2000, which removed him from his director position, violated legal provisions and deprived him of rights such as the distribution of investment returns. He requested a declaration that the board resolution in question is void and demanded that Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe jointly and severally compensate him for economic losses equivalent to his investment returns. Although the legal relationships underlying these two claims are different, they are both based on the same factual background that Xu Minghong considers himself an actual investor in Quanzhou Nanming Company and that his investment rights were improperly taken. Article 221 of the Civil Procedure Law Judicial Interpretation states: "If disputes based on the same facts arise, and the parties separately file lawsuits in the same People's Court, the People's Court may consolidate the cases for trial." The First Instance Court, finding that Xu Minghong's claims against Quanzhou Nanming Company and Lin Shuzhe were based on the same facts, determined that both claims were disputes related to the company and heard them together. This is legally sound, and this Court upholds it. The appellee, Lin Shuzhe, argues that the two claims in this case belong to different legal relationships and should not be heard together; this argument cannot stand and is not supported by this Court.

3. Regarding whether Xu Minghong is a qualified plaintiff in this case. Article 1 of the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (IV)" (hereinafter "Company Law Judicial Interpretation (IV)") provides that if a shareholder, director, supervisor, or other person of a company requests a declaration that a shareholders' meeting or board of directors' resolution is void or does not exist, the People's Court shall accept the case in accordance with the law. This provision expressly lists shareholders, directors, supervisors, etc., as plaintiffs in lawsuits for declaring company resolutions void and requires that "the People's Court shall accept the case in accordance with the law." According to Article 119, Item 1 of the Civil Procedure Law and Article 208, Paragraph 3 of the Civil Procedure Law Judicial Interpretation, the plaintiff filing the lawsuit must be "a citizen, legal person, or other organization that has a direct interest in the case." If, after accepting the case, the People's Court finds that the plaintiff's lawsuit does not meet the conditions for filing, it shall rule to dismiss the lawsuit. Accordingly, for a lawsuit filed by a shareholder, director, supervisor, etc., seeking to declare a company resolution void, the People's Court must apply both the Company Law and its judicial interpretations, and also examine whether the plaintiff has a "direct interest in the case" in accordance with the Civil Procedure Law and its judicial interpretations. By the same reasoning, a plaintiff filing a lawsuit for company profit distribution must also have shareholder status or have another direct interest in the company's profit distribution. Therefore, the First Instance Court, after accepting this case, lawfully examined whether Xu Minghong had a direct interest in this case and determined whether Xu Minghong had the standing to bring the two claims in this case. This application of law is correct.

   (1) Regarding whether Xu Minghong is a qualified plaintiff in the lawsuit for declaring the board resolution in question void. In this case, Xu Minghong requests a declaration that the board resolution in question is void on the grounds that the "Resolution of the Board of Directors of Quanzhou Nanming Entertainment Co., Ltd." dated August 9, 2000, unlawfully removed him from his director position. According to the facts found, at the time the board resolution in question was made, Quanzhou Nanming Company was a Sino-foreign equity joint venture. Article 6 of the "Law of the People's Republic of China on Sino-foreign Equity Joint Ventures" provides that a joint venture shall have a board of directors, the number of members of which shall be determined by the parties to the venture through consultation and specified in the contract and articles of association, and such directors shall be appointed and replaced by the parties to the venture; the board of directors shall have the authority to discuss and decide all major issues of the joint venture in accordance with the provisions of the articles of association. According to Article 19 and Article 21 of Chapter 4 of the Articles of Association of Quanzhou Nanming Company, the board of directors shall consist of eight directors, of which Licheng Company appoints two, Beifeng Company appoints two, and Hong Kong Nanming Company appoints four; when appointing or replacing directors, the three parties shall notify the board of directors in writing. Accordingly, the directors of Quanzhou Nanming Company are appointed and replaced by the parties to the joint venture. As a party to the joint venture, Hong Kong Nanming Company could appoint Xu Minghong as a director of Quanzhou Nanming Company and could also unilaterally remove Xu Minghong from his director position. Therefore, from the time Hong Kong Nanming Company's "Letter of Appointment" dated August 9, 2000, which included the removal of Xu Minghong from his director position, arrived at Quanzhou Nanming Company, Xu Minghong no longer held the position of director of Quanzhou Nanming Company. Although the board resolution in question contained the content of Xu Minghong's removal from the director position, its basis was the notice from the shareholder Hong Kong Nanming Company regarding the removal of Xu Minghong's director position. It merely reflected the will of the shareholder of the joint venture, not the will of the board of directors of Quanzhou Nanming Company. Therefore, this part of the content is merely a record by the board of directors of Quanzhou Nanming Company of an existing legal fact. According to the Company Law, as the company's operational decision-making body, the board of directors may, in accordance with the authority and voting procedures provided by law or the company's articles of association, form board resolutions after voting on matters under its consideration. However, such resolutions should reflect the board's commercial judgment and independent will. Consequently, the resolutions that shareholders, directors, supervisors, etc., may request to be declared void under Article 1 of the Company Law Judicial Interpretation (IV) do not include the recording document in this case that does not reflect the will of the board. Therefore, the part of the document in question concerning Xu Minghong's removal from the director position of Quanzhou Nanming Company, although bearing the name of a board resolution, does not constitute a board resolution within the meaning of the Company Law. In summary, the board resolution in question was not the cause of Xu Minghong's loss of his director position at Quanzhou Nanming Company. Regardless of whether the signature "Xu Mingliang" on the board resolution was forged, it does not affect the validity of Hong Kong Nanming Company's removal of his director position. Xu Minghong's appeal argument that he is a qualified plaintiff in the lawsuit for declaring the board resolution void cannot stand. The First Instance Court's ruling that Xu Minghong does not have a direct interest in the board resolution in question and is not a qualified plaintiff in this case is correct, and this Court upholds it.

   (2) Regarding whether Xu Minghong has a direct interest in the profit distribution of Quanzhou Nanming Company. Xu Minghong is not a shareholder of Quanzhou Nanming Company. In this case, he claims to be an actual investor of Quanzhou Nanming Company and requests to distribute company profits in proportion to his capital contribution. An actual investor under the Company Law is a civil subject who, in the name of a nominal shareholder, within the scope of that nominal shareholder's capital contribution obligation, invests funds, physical objects, etc., and ultimately enjoys investment returns. According to Article 24, Paragraph 1 of the "Provisions of the Supreme People's Court on Several Issues Concerning the Application of the Company Law of the People's Republic of China (III)" (hereinafter "Company Law Judicial Interpretation (III)") and Article 15, Paragraph 1 of the "Foreign Investment Judicial Interpretation (I)", an investor who is an actual investor must enter into a contract with the nominal shareholder, with the nominal investor as the nominal shareholder and the actual investor investing and enjoying the investment returns. Accordingly, to determine whether Xu Minghong's claim that he is an actual investor of Quanzhou Nanming Company can be established, it is necessary to examine whether the evidence he provided in this case can prove that there was an entrusted investment contract relationship between him and Hong Kong Nanming Company, with Hong Kong Nanming Company as the nominal shareholder and Xu Minghong as the actual investor. Hong Kong Nanming Company was registered and established in Hong Kong on January 12, 1993, with registered shareholders Xu Mingqi and Yang Lianjia, each holding one share. According to the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Property Co., Ltd." dated October 4, 1996, which Xu Minghong submitted to the First Instance, six parties, including Xu Minghong, Liu Sanhuang, Lin Wenlong, Huang Chaoyang, Dai Xinmin, and Hong Kong Southern Textile Co., Ltd., collectively raised HKD 25 million in proportion to their respective shares to form Hong Kong Nanming Company as a cooperative venture. Regarding whether the purpose of the six parties, including Xu Minghong, in raising funds was specifically for Hong Kong Nanming Company to fulfill its capital contribution obligations to Quanzhou Nanming Company, this board resolution does not contain a clear record. However, considering the amount of the agreed joint fund-raising of HKD 25 million, it is clearly greater than Hong Kong Nanming Company's subscribed capital contribution obligation to Quanzhou Nanming Company, which was RMB 14 million. The existing evidence in this case cannot prove the fact to be proven, i.e., that there was an entrusted investment relationship among Xu Minghong and the other five parties and Hong Kong Nanming Company, with Hong Kong Nanming Company as the nominal shareholder investing in Quanzhou Nanming Company. Therefore, Xu Minghong's claim, based on the subsequent fact that his capital contribution was actually used for Quanzhou Nanming Company, that he is an actual investor of that company lacks factual and legal basis and is not accepted by this Court. At the same time, an actual investor is not a shareholder of a foreign-invested enterprise. The law protects only the investment returns enjoyed by the actual investor based on a contractual arrangement with the nominal shareholder, not all the rights that a shareholder can enjoy. Therefore, Article 24, Paragraph 2 of the Company Law Judicial Interpretation (III) and Article 15, Paragraph 2 of the Foreign Investment Judicial Interpretation (I) both emphasize that the way for an actual investor to obtain investment returns is to claim against the nominal shareholder based on the contractual relationship between them. Article 17 of the Foreign Investment Judicial Interpretation (I) provides: "If an actual investor directly requests profit distribution or exercises other shareholder rights from a foreign-invested enterprise based on an agreement with the nominal shareholder of the foreign-invested enterprise, the People's Court will not support it." It can be seen that even if Xu Minghong's claim that there was an entrusted investment relationship with Hong Kong Nanming Company, referred to as an "investment channel," which made him an actual investor of Quanzhou Nanming Company, were established, he still could not directly claim investment returns from Quanzhou Nanming Company. From the above, the First Instance Court's ruling that Xu Minghong is not an actual investor of Quanzhou Nanming Company and that he does not have a direct interest in the profit distribution of Quanzhou Nanming Company is correct, and this Court upholds it. It is noted, however, that Article 216 of the Company Law provides: "Actual controller refers to a person who is not a shareholder of the company but who can actually control the company's behavior through investment relationships, agreements, or other arrangements." The First Instance Court, without examining the ownership of control over Quanzhou Nanming Company, made a finding that the six parties, including Xu Minghong, jointly contributed capital as the actual controller of Quanzhou Nanming Company. This finding lacks factual basis, and this Court corrects it.

4. Regarding whether there is a direct interest between Xu Minghong and Lin Shuzhe. As stated above, Xu Minghong is not a qualified plaintiff in the lawsuit for declaring the board resolution in question void. Lin Shuzhe, as the Chairman of the Board of Directors of Quanzhou Nanming Company, signed the board resolution in question as an act of performing his duties. Such conduct cannot, as a matter of law, give rise to personal liability on the part of Lin Shuzhe. Furthermore, since Xu Minghong has no direct interest relationship with Quanzhou Nanming Company and is not a qualified plaintiff in the lawsuit for profit distribution, Lin Shuzhe, as the legal representative of Quanzhou Nanming Company, is naturally not a qualified defendant in this case. Therefore, the First Instance Court's ruling dismissing Xu Minghong's lawsuit against Lin Shuzhe is correct in its outcome, and this Court upholds it.

5. Regarding the disposition of other related issues in this case. According to the contents recorded in the "Minutes of the First Board Meeting of Hong Kong Nanming Property Co., Ltd.", Xu Minghong and the other five parties jointly formed Hong Kong Nanming Company as a cooperative venture and contributed capital in proportion to their respective shares. This board minutes also recorded the share percentages of the six parties and the dates of investment. Furthermore, in the litigation of this case, Xu Minghong claimed that the six parties invested externally according to their agreement with Hong Kong Nanming Company. Therefore, legal relationships were formed between Xu Minghong and the other five parties, and between the six parties and Hong Kong Nanming Company. Xu Minghong should assert and exercise his corresponding rights based on the agreements with the other five parties and the agreements between the six parties and Hong Kong Nanming Company. Since Xu Minghong's investment situation in the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region does not affect the determination of whether Xu Minghong has the standing as a plaintiff in this case, this Court will not adjudicate the nature of the legal relationships between Xu Minghong and the other five parties, nor between the six parties and Hong Kong Nanming Company. By the same reasoning, it is also unnecessary for the First Instance Court to examine and determine in this case whether there were financial transactions between Xu Minghong and Hong Kong Nanming Company, the specific amounts of such transactions, or whether such funds constituted direct investments in Hong Kong Nanming Company. This Court does not confirm the First Instance Court's findings regarding the above content. Xu Minghong may request the court hearing his separate rights claim to examine and determine these issues. Additionally, since this case does not require a substantive examination of Xu Minghong's claims, the matters involved in Xu Minghong's First Instance application for witnesses to testify do not affect the determination of the standing to sue in this case. The First Instance Court's denial of his applications for investigation and evidence collection, handwriting authentication, entrusted audit, and witness testimony was not improper; this Court also does not permit Xu Minghong's applications for investigation and evidence collection and entrusted appraisal made during the second instance. As for the relevant evidence submitted by Xu Minghong during the second instance, even if it were admitted, it would not prove that he has the standing as a plaintiff, and this Court does not find it relevant in this case.

In conclusion, Xu Minghong's appeal cannot stand. The First Instance ruling found the relevant facts clearly and applied the law correctly. In accordance with Article 170, Paragraph 1, Item 1 and Article 171 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the ruling is as follows:

Appeal dismissed; the First Instance ruling is affirmed. This ruling is final.
